sections.title: What is a Monotonic Queue?
sections.content:
A monotonic queue is a **double-ended queue (deque)** that maintains its elements in either strictly increasing or strictly decreasing order of their values. Unlike a regular queue, elements can be removed from both ends. This structure answers **range min/max queries over a sliding window** in O(1) per query, with O(n) total work across all queries.

The key distinction from a monotonic stack is what the data structure is tracking: a monotonic **stack** processes a sequence once and answers "what is the next/previous greater or smaller element?" - a neighbor relationship. A monotonic **queue** maintains a window sliding over the sequence and answers "what is the maximum or minimum in the current window?" - a range relationship over time.

The deque stores **indices**, not values. This is essential: indices let you check whether the front element has fallen outside the current window (expired) and evict it. When a new element arrives, dominated elements - those at the back that are smaller than the new element for a max-queue - are removed because they can never be the window maximum while the new element is still in the window. Each index is added once and removed at most once, giving **O(n) total** work regardless of window size.

Beyond the canonical Sliding Window Maximum problem, the monotonic queue appears as a DP optimization. When a recurrence is `dp[i] = max(dp[j]) + cost` for j in some sliding range of i, a monotonic queue maintains that max efficiently, reducing O(n²) DP to O(n). This appears in Jump Game VI, Constrained Subset Sum, and Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K.

sections.title: When to Use This
sections.content: Use a monotonic queue when you need the minimum or maximum value in a fixed-size or bounded sliding window, and you cannot afford O(k) to scan the window each time. Also use it when a DP recurrence requires the max or min of a range of previous dp values - the queue maintains that range optimally. If queries are static (no sliding), use a sparse table instead.
signals: maximum of every window of size k
DP with max or min over sliding range of states
shortest subarray with sum at least k

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
## Deque Invariant and Two Eviction Types

The deque stores indices. For a **max-queue** (sliding window maximum), the invariant is: elements in the deque are in **decreasing** order of their values. For a **min-queue**, they are in increasing order.

Two types of eviction happen at different ends:

1. **Expiry eviction (front)** - check if `deque[front] <= i - k` (the front index has slid out of the window). Pop from the front. This keeps the window boundary correct.

2. **Dominance eviction (back)** - before pushing the new index `i`, pop from the back while `arr[deque[back]] <= arr[i]` (for max-queue). These back elements are dominated by `arr[i]` - as long as `arr[i]` is in the window, they can never be the maximum.

After both evictions, push `i` to the back. The front of the deque is always the index of the current window's maximum.

## Sliding Window Maximum Algorithm

For an array of size n and window size k:
1. For each index `i` from 0 to n-1:
   - Pop from **front** while `deque[front] <= i - k` (expired)
   - Pop from **back** while `arr[deque[back]] <= arr[i]` (dominated)
   - Push `i` to back
   - If `i >= k - 1`, record `arr[deque[0]]` as the current window max
2. Result has `n - k + 1` elements

Total: O(n) - each index is pushed and popped at most once across the entire traversal.

## Monotonic Queue as DP Optimization

When dp[i] depends on the max of dp[j] for j in [i-k, i-1], maintain a decreasing monotonic queue of dp values. As i advances, the valid range [i-k, i-1] slides forward - evict dp values falling outside the left boundary from the front, evict dominated dp values from the back when a new dp[i] is computed.

Example - Jump Game VI: `dp[i] = max(dp[i-k], ..., dp[i-1]) + nums[i]`. Naive: O(n*k). With monotonic queue: O(n).

## Monotonic Queue vs Monotonic Stack

| | Monotonic Stack | Monotonic Queue |
|---|---|---|
| Structure | Single-end stack | Double-end deque |
| Query | Next/prev greater/smaller | Window min/max |
| Eviction | One type (dominance from top) | Two types (expiry from front, dominance from back) |
| Use case | Neighbor relationships | Sliding window relationships |

sections.title: Core Template
sections.explanation: The first function is the canonical sliding window maximum using a decreasing deque of indices. The second shows the DP optimization pattern - maintaining a window of past dp values using the same deque structure.

items.name: Sliding Window Minimum
items.description: Identical structure to sliding window maximum - flip the dominance eviction direction. Pop from the back while `arr[deque[back]] >= arr[i]` instead of `<=`. The front is now the index of the current window minimum.

items.name: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K
items.description: Apply a monotonic deque to the prefix sum array. Maintain an increasing deque of prefix sum indices. For each new prefix sum, pop from the front while `prefixSum[i] - prefixSum[deque[front]] >= k` and track the shortest valid subarray. O(n).
items.example_problem: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K

items.name: Jump Game VI
items.description: DP recurrence `dp[i] = max(dp[i-k..i-1]) + nums[i]`. The max over a sliding window of dp values is exactly the monotonic queue problem. Reduces from O(n*k) naive DP to O(n).

items.name: Constrained Subsequence Sum
items.description: Find maximum sum of a subsequence where adjacent picked elements are at most k apart. DP with monotonic queue: `dp[i] = max(dp[max(0,i-k)..i-1]) + nums[i]` (only take positive contributions). Same sliding window DP optimization.

sections.title: Complexity
sections.explanation: Each of the n elements is pushed into the deque exactly once and popped at most once (either via expiry or dominance eviction). So the total number of push+pop operations across all n iterations is at most 2n - O(n) overall regardless of window size k. The deque holds at most k elements at any time (one full window), so space is O(k). This is a major improvement over the O(n*k) naive approach of scanning each window.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Storing values instead of indices in the deque - values alone cannot check expiry (`deque[front] <= i - k` requires the index, not the value); always store indices and use `arr[deque[front]]` to read the corresponding value.

Evicting expired elements from the back instead of the front - expiry (window boundary) check must happen at the front; dominance eviction happens at the back. Mixing these two directions corrupts the deque invariant entirely.

Off-by-one in expiry condition - the window of size k centered ending at `i` covers indices `[i-k+1, i]`, so index `i-k` is just outside the left boundary. Evict when `deque[front] <= i - k` (strictly expired), not `< i - k`.

Recording the answer before the first full window - start recording results only when `i >= k - 1`. Recording from `i = 0` adds partial-window maximums that are meaningless and shifts the result array.

Confusing monotonic queue with monotonic stack - a stack cannot evict expired elements (it has no front access); using a stack for sliding window max means old elements that left the window still influence the 'maximum', producing wrong answers.

items.why: The canonical monotonic queue problem - directly applies the decreasing deque with front expiry and back dominance eviction.

items.title: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K
items.why: Tests applying monotonic queue to a prefix sum array - non-obvious mapping where the deque tracks increasing prefix sums to find shortest valid subarray.

items.title: Jump Game VI
items.why: Tests the DP + monotonic queue optimization pattern - max over a sliding range of previous dp values.

items.title: Constrained Subsequence Sum
items.why: Tests monotonic queue DP with a variable window constraint - combines the greedy of only taking positive dp values with the sliding window max.

sections.title: What to Learn Next
sections.why: Monotonic queue gives O(1) amortized range min/max for a sliding window on a dynamic stream. Sparse table gives O(1) worst-case range min/max for static arrays with no updates. Learning sparse table completes the picture of range query techniques across different data conditions.
